articles.title: Fiery Georgia Senate debate gets personal: 4 takeaways
articles.summary: The first debate for Georgia Senate on Thursday evening quickly devolved into a string of personal attacks and campaign talking points as Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) and Rep. Mike Collins (R) wrestle for voters’ support in the closely-watched midterm race. The incumbent Democrat has maintained a lead over his GOP challenger in recent polling, but…
articles.body:
The first debate for Georgia Senate on Thursday evening quickly devolved into a string of personal attacks and campaign talking points as Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) and Rep. Mike Collins (R) wrestle for voters’ support in the closely-watched midterm race.

The incumbent Democrat has maintained a lead over his GOP challenger in recent polling, but Republicans are still holding out hope to flip this seat in November.

The candidates faced questions during the Atlanta News First debate in Atlanta about their stance on a range of issues, including artificial intelligence, border security, rural health care and agriculture.

Repeatedly, Collins and Ossoff used their allotted time to criticize each other’s family backgrounds and argue that their opponent was not fit to represent Georgia on Capitol Hill.

Here are four takeaways from their first face off:

The Democratic incumbent referred to Collins several times on Thursday evening as “the bigot congressman,” an insult he has repeatedly invoked on the campaign trail.

Ossoff pointed to the lawmaker’s past controversial social media posts, including a sharing a video from the University of Mississippi in 2024 in which a Black woman is surrounded by white students who are mimicking ape-like motions and making monkey sounds.

Collins captioned the post, “Ole Miss taking care of business.”

“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club,” Ossoff said in reference to the post.

The senator also accused the Republican of promoting “Neo-Nazi propaganda,” pointing to social media posts made by his son-in-law and a former staffer.

“It’s not just that you hired half the Third Reich to staff your congressional office and you have promoted Neo-Nazi content online. It’s that you’re robbing your constituents to subsidize your donors,” Ossoff said during his response to a question about data centers.

Collins responded to a moderator question about his son-in-law’s posts, saying he “condemned racism, anti-Semitism, hate.”

“I don’t care where the source is, and I tell him that too. It’s wrong,” he said.

Collins attacks Democrat as ‘trust fund kid’

The Republican nominee called his opponent a “trust fund kid,” arguing he’s unable to understand the affordability issues faced by people in the state.

Collins reupped this criticism in response to a debate question about financial troubles facing rural hospitals in the state.

“You know the problem is, and Jon Ossoff won’t understand this because he doesn’t have to worry about health care,” he said. “He doesn’t have to worry about trying to buy health care insurance for his family. He never will.”

Ossoff hit back, claiming his opponent “inherited a seat in Congress” during his closing statement. The Republican’s father is Mac Collins, the late Georgia lawmaker who served 12 years in the House.

Collins and Ossoff hit one another over their legislative record on affordability, as rising costs of living across the country remain top of mind for voters ahead of Election Day.

The Democrat pointed to rising diesel and fertilizer costs amid the Iran war and the Trump administration’s tariffs.

“As we speak right now, it’s Georgia farmers bearing the brunt of the Mike Collins-Donald Trump tariffs,” Ossoff said. “Just like it’s Georgia farmers bearing the brunt of these high diesel prices.

The Republican nominee placed blame on last year’s government shutdown, which he and other congressional lawmakers have accused Democrats of causing.

“He shut it down, y’all,” Collins said. “Right when we were trying to get that emergency money out for Hurricane Helene so that our farmers and our small communities could repair and prepare for this year’s harvest.”

Collins skirts question about 2020 election

Ossoff put his opponent on the spot during Thursday’s debate about his support for President Trump’s unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud in the 2020 presidential election, including in Georgia’s Fulton County.

“Mike Collins is one of the most extreme members of Congress,” the Democrat said. “He’s a Trump puppet election denier. I want to hear if Mike still believes the 2020 election was stolen. What do you say, Mike?”

Ossoff turned to face his opponent, who stared down at his notes before a moderator asked him a new question about The Laken Riley Act he introduced.

articles.body:
President Trump said Thursday that Minnesotans should “fight back” against Somali immigrants following previous attacks against the group.

“The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants. There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . “The people of Minnesota must fight back.”

He added that Minnesota’s residents were “abandoned” by the state government, and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D) was “an incompetent thief who doesn’t want to get involved.”

“[Walz] just wants to get out of town with as much as he can steal, and then, lead a quiet life,” Trump continued. “The Somalians should not be allowed to get away with what they are doing. They view you as weak and stupid people. Fight back Minnesota, fight back! If you need, the Federal Government will come to your rescue.”

“Governor Tim Walz, and Mayor of Minneapolis, Jacob Frey, must immediately ask for Federal help — and leave the rest to us,” he concluded.

The Somali community has been targeted by the Trump administration due to a massive pandemic-era fraud scheme that stole hundreds of millions from a federally funded nutrition program. As much as $1 billion is reported to have been stolen in separate plots.

Trump previously slammed the Somali community in 2025, referring to Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar (D) as “ garbage ,” and that Somalia “stinks.”

The Trump administration ended temporary protected status (TPS) for Somali holders in January. Former Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Kristi Noem said at the time that continuing TPS protections were “contrary to our national interests.”

Walz accused Trump in 2025 of “ demonizing ” Somali migrants in Minnesota.

“As far as demonizing our Somali community, maybe, he could help us on some things,” Walz said at the time. “Demonizing an entire community, folks who are in the professions, educators, artists, doctors, lawyers, entrepreneurs, they bring the diversity and the energy to a place like Minnesota.”

According to World Population Review , Minnesota has the largest population of Somalis at 1.07 percent concentrated primarily in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area. Most of the population arrived in the U.S. as refugees after a civil war in Somalia throughout the 1990s.

articles.title: Michigan Senate debate goes off the rails: 4 takeaways
articles.summary: Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s first Senate debate in Michigan turned so contentious it even extended off camera. “In 30 years of doing debates, I’ve never seen it continue during the commercial,” WOOD TV moderator Rick Albin said. “But it did” Rogers and El-Sayed participated in a debate hosted by Nexstar’s Grand Rapids…
articles.body:
Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s first Senate debate in Michigan turned so contentious it even extended off camera.

“In 30 years of doing debates, I’ve never seen it continue during the commercial,” WOOD TV moderator Rick Albin said. “But it did”

Rogers and El-Sayed participated in a debate hosted by Nexstar’s Grand Rapids station where the pair lobbed personal attacks centering on corporate and foreign influence, carpetbagging, President Trump and their professional careers.

El-Sayed looked to make the debate a referendum on the president by tying Rogers to Trump while the GOP candidate sought to cast himself as bipartisan while characterizing the Democrat as dishonest. Last month, the Democrat took the debate stage alone after Rogers declined to participate , accusing the host outlet of bias.

The pair will square off one more time before the election on Oct. 21 in a debate hosted by WXYZ-TV.

Here’s four takeaways from the first Michigan Senate debate:

The debate ended where it started — feisty and spirited — as the two men immediately launched into personal attacks.

El-Sayed chided Rogers at multiple points, telling him to “be serious, my guy” while suggesting the former congressman was beholden to the president. The former Wayne County health official also brought up Rogers’ past Florida residence, suggesting he was a carpetbagger.

“I’ve been absolutely clear. I want our tax dollars spent here to provide schools here, and by here, I mean Michigan, not Florida,” El-Sayed said during the debate when asked if he would vote to provide Israel with defensive arms if attacked.

The Democrat described Rogers as a “rubber stamp” for Trump that is beholden to corporate interests.

Meanwhile, Rogers suggested that El-Sayed, who received a medical degree from Columbia University and a doctorate in public health at Oxford University, was falsely parading as a medical professional. El-Sayed has previously received scrutiny for calling himself a “physician” despite not practicing medicine.

“And the doctor — well, he’s not really a doctor.” Rogers said during the debate.

“Matter of fact, if somebody came into his office and he tried to treat that patient, he’d go to jail. So, listen to this guy and what he’s trying to sell here today,” Rogers added later.

Rogers also baselessly alleged that El-Sayed and his family have ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. Bridge Michigan reported last month that there was no evidence that El-Sayed has direct ties to the group.

The Republican appeared at one point to almost go as far as to suggest that El-Sayed, who is Muslim, could have terrorist family relatives.

“Those programs were really, really important in catching people who were suspected of terrorists and being terrorist — committing a terrorist act, that’s really, really important,” Rogers said when asked about his position of guardrails on flock cameras.

“And why would that bother you? Well, if you have someone in your family that might be on —” Rogers added, before El-Sayed, chimed in.

“Go ahead and say it,” El-Sayed said at one point, adding, “You’ve been tiptoeing around it the whole time, just say it.”

The progressive frequently invoked the president, as Republican candidates across the country grapple with Trump’s underwater approval ratings.

“It’s about whether or not you trust your next U.S. senator [to] stand up to Trump and Trumpism,” El-Sayed said.

“But when [you’re] running because Donald Trump called you and asked you to run, you can tell he’s not going to stand up to anybody,” he added

At another point, El-Sayed called Rogers a “sock puppet for the Trump administration” while talking about the Republican and Trump’s war in Iran.

The former congressman, who is endorsed by the president, has sought to walk a tight rope with Trump amid his unpopularity. Earlier this week, Rogers called for an end to the trade war with Canada , and he previously called for the conflict in Iran to come to an end.

During the debate, Rogers said he called Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and pushed for a deal on tariffs with Canada.

“I would like to see the deal made,” he said, later adding that, “Canada still has some high tariffs for U.S. goods, and they did it before this started. Those should be eliminated. There are tariffs that I think are too high and not helpful for us. We ought to get rid of those.”

Rogers: Minnesota immigration crackdown ‘not appropriate’

Another notable point during the debate was Rogers’s break with the Trump administration over its immigration crackdown , suggesting that actions taken by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Minnesota had gone too far.

“I think the public efforts in Minnesota were probably not appropriate. I actually did fugitive raids when I was an FBI agent in Chicago. You always want to go in quiet, get the bad guy, get out of the neighborhood for less problems,” Rogers said. “So that’s — that to me was something that they could have done differently.”

The former congressman suggested that they later corrected their tactics.

Several shootings involving federal immigration enforcement officers, including two in Minnesota, have sparked scrutiny of the Trump administration as critics have argued that the White House’s crackdown on immigration has gone too far. On Thursday, a man was shot by ICE in New York.

El-Sayed sidesteps question on Israel, Iran

El-Sayed avoided answering a question on whether he saw Iran or Israel as the bigger threat when pressed multiple times on the debate stage, before suggesting that both countries were “dangerous” to the U.S.

“I’m just going to say that that’s a ridiculous hypothetical because here’s what’s happening right now: Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran,” El-Sayed said. “We have watched as Iran has responded by bombing all kinds of countries in the Middle East and then choking off the world’s energy supply. So, this is a situation in which I don’t think we should be a part.”

Pressed again later, El-Sayed criticized the question before saying both were a threat.

“I think both of them have proven dangerous in their own way. One at risk of attacking us. One getting us into wars we have no business fighting,” he said.

articles.title: Second Maine Senate debate takes testy turn: 3 takeaways
articles.summary: Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson squared off Thursday in the second Maine Senate debate of the week, sparring over the Iran war and high prices as their battleground race barrels toward Election Day. The hourlong debate, hosted by WMTW, turned testy at times as the rivals defended their records and re-upped many…
articles.body:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson squared off Thursday in the second Maine Senate debate of the week, sparring over the Iran war and high prices as their battleground race barrels toward Election Day.

The hourlong debate, hosted by WMTW, turned testy at times as the rivals defended their records and re-upped many of their night-one talking points about abortion, immigration and the economy. Collins stressed that she’s often at odds with her party, while Jackson highlighted her alignment with President Trump.

The stakes were high for both candidates to avoid on-stage gaffes and snag strong clips that could move the needle of the close race. Decision Desk HQ’s polling averages show Jackson, who became the party’s pick after their initial nominee withdrew this summer, leading the five-term incumbent by just over a point in the blue-leaning Pine Tree State.

Here are three takeaways from the latest debate, with two more showdowns scheduled later this month:

Senate hopefuls battle over Iran war: ‘You owe me an apology’

The rivals clashed over remarks on the Iran war and its economic impacts on Mainers struggling under high prices.

As the candidates debated how to address record-high heating oil prices , moderator Jon Chrisos pressed Collins over her Senate votes on Trump’s military moves in Iran.

She stressed that she has “voted nine times to end this war” under the War Powers Act. A live fact-check from PolitiFact, though, called her claim “selective counting ,” pointing to five times Collins voted against such resolutions.

“She could use her leverage to stop this war. But instead, they’re making money,” Jackson argued during the debate. “I mean, Senator Collins and her husband [are] making money, more, off of this war, and so is a whole bunch of other people, and that’s why this doesn’t, doesn’t stop.”

“That is absolutely outrageous, and you owe me an apology,” the senator said.

“No, you owe me an apology,” Jackson replied.

Jackson did not offer specific evidence for his claim that Collins was profiting from the war.

PolitiFact noted that the senator’s husband, Thomas Daffron, owns stock in Boeing and RTX, both defense contractors for the U.S. Military, according to reporting from The Maine Independent. A spokesperson told the outlet last month that Collins has “never bought, sold or owned” any individual stock shares as senator, and that her husband’s investments “are made exclusively by a third-party advisor without his consultation.”

Jackson pointed to the war — which is deeply unpopular among midterm voters — at multiple points in the night, stressing that “we have to get out of Iran” to bring down fuel prices, and raising concerns that “people will freeze to death this winter because they can’t afford to heat their home.”

Collins, though, cast doubt on the Iran war as the main driver of high electric rates in Maine, casting blame on moves from the state Legislature, where Jackson served as Senate president.

“It’s just not accurate to say that it’s the Iran war that has caused Maine to have the fourth highest electric bills in the country. If it were the Iran War, why wouldn’t New Hampshire and other states have the same level of electric bills that Maine has?” Collins asked.

Thirty years ago, Collins pledged she would only serve for two terms if elected to the Senate. Now, she’s going for a sixth six-year term.

“What I learned is how much more effective I could be as the seventh ranked person in the Senate versus 99th, which is what I was when I first started out,” Collins said, when asked on the debate stage about what changed her mind.

Touting some of her more recent legislative achievements, including becoming the first Maine senator to chair the powerful Appropriations Committee, she said “I couldn’t have done this in the early years in the Senate.”

Collins was reelected in 2014 by nearly 40 points, but won her 2020 bid by a comparatively slim 9 points. She’s now considered one of the most vulnerable senators in the 2026 cycle.

But Jackson also faced questions about what was behind his bid. After running unsuccessfully for governor this cycle, the Democrat was named as his party’s replacement nominee after Graham Platner, a progressive oyster farmer who won the initial primary, withdrew amid sexual misconduct allegations.

“Why should voters see this as your own campaign and not something that you inherited?” Chrisos asked.

“Well, it isn’t my own campaign. I mean, it’s the people across Maine,” Jackson replied. “This is not about Troy Jackson. It’s not about Graham Platner. What it is about is Donald Trump and Susan Collins and the band that are making life so much harder in the state.”

Collins, Jackson respond to controversial reports

Both candidates responded to recent reports that have raised questions about both candidates’ financial moves in the run-up to Election Day.

Collins denied recent reporting that accused her of receiving illegal campaign contributions, calling the claims “absolutely false.”

ProPublica reported in September that, after a former CEO of defense contractor Navatak made a 2019 donation to a Collins super PAC, Collins used her position on the Appropriations Committee to award military contracts to the company.

Martin Kao pleaded guilty in 2022 to making illegal campaign contributions. The FBI at the time found nothing implicating Collins or her campaign — but Chrisos questioned what Collins would say to voters who think the report raises questions about her campaign financing.

“Well, they don’t, and these allegations are absolutely false, and they’ve been proven false. But Troy and Chuck Schumer keep running false ads to try to convince you otherwise,” Collins said.

She said that the University of Maine had come to her with a proposal for research with Navatek, and that Kao is “in jail today, where he belongs.”

Jackson, too, responded to new reporting about donations to a PAC he was involved in during his service in the Maine Legislature.

The Washington Post reported that, up until two years ago, the Democrat used a PAC that accepted funds from tobacco, pharmaceutical and other big companies and affiliated PACs — though he openly rejects corporate PAC money in the Senate race.

Asked what he’d say to voters who think his role in the PAC raises questions, Jackson said that the PAC “is a group of people.”

“I didn’t make decisions on who or what, when we were going to take money,” he said.

articles.title: Arlington County sues to block Trump arch after project gets key approval
articles.summary: Arlington County has filed a lawsuit to block President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch following the project’s approval by the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts in April. The lawsuit opposed the construction of the proposed 250-foot arch, citing concerns about the project’s impact on tourism and safety to local residents. “Using the Arch to store large…
articles.body:
Arlington County has filed a lawsuit to block President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch following the project’s approval by the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts in April.

The lawsuit opposed the construction of the proposed 250-foot arch, citing concerns about the project’s impact on tourism and safety to local residents.

“Using the Arch to store large stockpiles of ammunition and as a staging point for drones and snipers, so close to commuters and tourists, will dramatically worsen these public-safety harms and the risk of accidents,” attorneys for Arlington County wrote in a complaint .

“The Arch will…directly obstruct the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery that was deliberately created to symbolize the nation’s post-Civil War reunification,” the lawyers continued.

The legal team stated that Arlington County’s 245,000 residents would be “harmed by increased traffic” near the project’s site at Memorial Circle.

The lawsuit named the Department of the Interior and its Secretary Doug Burgum alongside the National Park Service (NPS) and acting director Jessica Bowron as defendants.

“At a time when millions of Americans are struggling to make ends meet, we don’t need vanity projects. This project will do significant harm to the people of Arlington County,” Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward, an organization suing with the county, said in a press release on Thursday.

This is not the first lawsuit against the proposed arch, as a group of Vietnam War veterans sued in September for an emergency court order to block the project from breaking ground.

They also sued in February , similarly arguing that the location of the arch would block historical sightlines between the Lincoln Memorial, Arlington National Cemetery and Arlington House.

The NPS backed the arch’s proposed location earlier this fall, but also found the monument would have “ adverse effects ” on several historic sites as well as the skyline of the nation’s capital.

The arch is one of Trump’s projects as part of his efforts to “Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful Again.” Other projects included renovations at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool , an ongoing legal battle over changes to the Kennedy Center and choosing to pave over the White House Rose Garden .

articles.title: Brazilian Supreme Court judge issues arrest warrant for Eduardo Bolsonaro
articles.summary: Arrest warrant for presidential candidate’s brother is issued weeks before Brazil’s runoff election.
articles.body:
A Brazilian Supreme Court justice has issued an arrest warrant for Eduardo Bolsonaro , brother of presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, a move likely to heat up the hard-fought race.

Justice Alexandre de Moraes issued the arrest warrant on Thursday, weeks before a runoff election for the country’s presidency between incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro, the favourite to win .

In June, the Brazilian Supreme Court convicted Eduardo Bolsonaro on charges of lobbying the US to interfere in the trial of his father, former right-wing President Jair Bolsonaro.

Eduardo Bolsonaro has been a key link between his brother and the Trump administration, accompanying him to a May meeting with US President Donald Trump at the White House.

Both sides of Brazil’s deeply polarised partisan divide have long accused each other of corruption and lawfare as political drama reaches a crescendo in the buildup to the October 25 runoff.

In March 2025, Eduardo Bolsonaro pledged he would move to the US full time to “focus 100 percent” of his energy on freeing his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.

The move cost him his seat in the Brazilian National Congress and his job as a federal police investigator.

The 42-year-old former lawmaker lives in Texas and is a green card holder.

He was convicted of lobbying to impose sanctions on members of the Brazilian government and to implement higher tariffs on the country’s exports during the trial of his father.

De Moraes, whom the Bolsonaro family regards as a political enemy, chaired the investigation that led to Jair Bolsonaro being sentenced in September 2025 to 27 years in prison for plotting to stage a coup.

The justice said in his ruling that Eduardo Bolsonaro should start serving his four-year sentence immediately.

“The defendant cannot benefit from his own wrongdoing by fleeing the national territory to an unknown location for the purpose of thwarting the application of criminal law,” de Moraes said.

De Moraes also cancelled Eduardo Bolsonaro’s Brazilian passport and instructed the country’s federal police to arrest him if he returns to Brazil.

images.caption: Eduardo Bolsonaro speaks next to an image of his father, former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro [File: Tomas Cuesta/Getty Images]
